claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase lamellar microstructure consisting of a ductile FCC phase and a harder BCC or ordered phase.
Controlled directional solidification can refine the alloy's lamellar spacing by tailoring its cooling rate.
A post-solidification annealing treatment can improve coherency between the two phases.
Directional solidification followed by annealing will produce optimized interlamellar spacing and improved interphase-interface coherency.
A refined lamellar architecture distributes applied loads more uniformly.
Refined lamellae and their interfaces impede dislocation motion through enhanced barrier effects.
Improved phase boundaries delay crack initiation.
The proposed microstructural changes mitigate the conventional strength–ductility trade-off.
Relative to the as-cast state, the combined treatment will increase yield strength.
Relative to the as-cast state, the combined treatment will increase ultimate tensile strength.
Relative to the as-cast state, the combined treatment will increase total elongation.
The simultaneous strength and ductility improvement should occur under ambient-temperature loading in compositionally similar, dual-phase eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on solidification cooling rate and annealing temperature and duration.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis distinguishes yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation, but the falsification rule ambiguously equates 'yield strength and ductility' with 'ultimate tensile strength and elongation.' Ultimate tensile strength is a strength metric rather than a ductility metric, so the required outcome variables are inconsistently mapped.
